proposals.diff_summary: Every dev-created PR is built in a dev-workflow-mandated isolated worktree (.claude/worktrees/agent-<branch>/) that stays checked out after the PR opens, so a worktree-owned branch can never be deleted by `git branch -d` while that worktree exists. `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch` therefore reliably fails its branch-delete step with 'used by worktree' -- 45 occurrences across 5 of the 10 sampled sessions, and 2 of those sessions also chained a 'the head branch is not up to date with the base branch' failure immediately before it (requiring a `gh api -X PUT .../update-branch` call and a re-poll of CI on the new head SHA). Each occurrence currently gets re-diagnosed from scratch: a failed merge call, a separate `gh pr view --json state,mergedAt` just to confirm the squash-merge itself (which did succeed) actually landed despite the misleading top-level error, then -- often in a later, disconnected turn -- a manual `git worktree remove <path> --force` and `git branch -d <branch>`. Add a bullet to section 6 ('Reviewer mechanics and blind spots') naming this as an expected, routine two-step merge sequence for any worktree-built PR rather than a problem to diagnose: (1) if `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch` errors only on the branch-delete line, the merge already succeeded -- confirm via `gh pr view <N> --json state,mergedAt` only if genuinely unsure, don't treat it as a failure to retry; (2) if the error instead says the head branch is not up to date, run `gh api -X PUT repos/{o}/{r}/pulls/<N>/update-branch`, wait for CI to re-run on the new head SHA (checks re-queue from scratch), then merge again; (3) clean up locally right away with `git worktree remove .claude/worktrees/agent-<branch> --force` followed by `git branch -d <branch>` -- safe once merged, since the worktree's content is already on master.
proposals.expected_impact: Removes the ~2-3 extra diagnostic tool calls (failed merge, state-confirmation query, later rediscovery of the worktree-lock cause) per worktree-built PR merge. At 45 observed occurrences across the sample, this is one of the highest-frequency repeated patterns found -- essentially every PR merge pays this tax today.

evidence.quote: please resume (user message, repeated verbatim 9 times across this span of turns, each time directed at a paused subagent that the PM had not yet proactively resumed)

proposals.diff_summary: agents/pm.md already documents one subagent-lifecycle edge case verbatim in its 'Behavioural rules' section (the 'Pause/stop/hold off includes work already in flight' paragraph) but has zero guidance for the far more frequent edge case actually observed: a spawned subagent pausing or being hard-terminated by a session rate limit mid-task. Today the PM waits for the user to notice the agent went quiet and type 'please resume' -- which happened 9 times in a row in one incident in the sampled session -- instead of checking agent status itself (ListAgents) and resuming proactively. No file under .claude/agents/ or agents/pm.md mentions rate limits, resume, or respawn at all (grep returned zero matches outside one unrelated example string). Add a paragraph to 'Behavioural rules', in the same style as the existing pause/stop paragraph: on noticing (or being told) a spawned subagent has gone idle, check whether it is a graceful pause (resumable in place via SendMessage to the same agent name/id) or a hard termination from a rate limit (not resumable by name -- respawn a fresh agent pointed at the same worktree path to continue, never re-spawn under the same name, which risks a duplicate running agent). Do this on your own initiative rather than waiting for the user to ask again.
proposals.expected_impact: Directly targets the 9 redundant user-authored 'please resume' turns observed in one incident (each one a full round trip: user message -> PM re-reads agent state -> SendMessage -> wait). Generalizing this into standing PM behavior should prevent the pattern recurring across future long-running delegation-heavy sessions, which this repo's workflow produces often (every epic spawns multiple long-lived subagents).
